Monitoring water resources

We’re the driest region in the UK, and with a fast-growing population, it's important that we monitor water resources closely to keep taps flowing and toilets flushing now and long into the future. That's why we're always exploring different ways to save and protect every drop. ​

The East of England has experienced an exceptionally dry year, with only around 39% of expected rainfall recorded during the spring and only 1% of the rainfall expected during July. During spring and summer there has been sustained periods of intense hot and dry weather and successive record-breaking heatwaves. These conditions have placed considerable pressure on both our water resources and the natural environment, with river flows across much of the region now notably or exceptionally low and reservoir storage reducing quickly during the summer period.

 

Throughout this period, our focus has been on maintaining reliable supplies for customers while protecting the environment on which those supplies ultimately depend. Our operational teams have been working around the clock to maximise water production, transfer water across our network, accelerate leakage activity, and support those areas experiencing the greatest demand. By using a little less to save every drop you can help too – small changes make a big difference.

 

Despite these efforts, demand for water has risen significantly (over 30% more water) during peak times and the underlying environmental conditions continue to deteriorate. We therefore concluded that introducing a Temporary Usage Ban was the responsible course of action. This action is helping to reduce demand, safeguard vulnerable river catchments and improve our ability to maintain resilient supplies during the summer. It’s the proactive and responsible approach to protect the environment and water supplies.

 

The Temporary Usage Ban (TUB) is in place across the region from Saturday 11 July 2026.

All the detail can be found on our Hosepipe Restrictions webpage.

Extra action needed in The Fens, King’s Lynn, Norwich and Norfolk

 

Although recent rainfall has helped, these areas are recovering from drought more slowly than others. The Rivers Wissey, Wensum and Nar are all still very low, so local water supplies and the environment still need extra protection.

 

If you live or work in these areas, please use water for essential purposes and put off non-essential tasks using water where you can.

The graphic below shows the current water resource levels across the region. Please note that we only receive all the data required to update this graphic in the middle of each month for the previous month.

Water Sources

Around half the water we supply comes from groundwater sources (e.g. boreholes) and the other half comes from surface water sources (e.g. reservoirs and rivers).

 

Groundwater

Groundwater moves below our feet in rocks, with levels typically rising when temperatures and evaporation is low and soils are wet.  The time taken for groundwater levels to respond to rainfall can range from hours to a few months, depending on the type of soil, rock and depth to groundwater. This water can be used by drilling holes (boreholes).

Rivers​

As well as abstracting water from rivers for storage in our reservoirs we can also abstract water from rivers to get directly pumped to our treating and cleaning works (we call these direct river intakes). We help manage our water supply by taking care and protecting over 3,000 km of rivers. 

Reservoirs​

We abstract water from rivers to fill our 6 key reservoirs around the region.

Scroll through the table below to view our weekly reservoir levels and whether they are above, below or at average levels for the time of year. The table is updated with data from the start of each week:

Your local sources​

We’re the largest water company by geographic area, and because the environments we cover are so different, some areas in our region may experience more challenges than others and react differently to weather conditions. For more information about your local water sources, find out where your water comes from.​
